reason: The provided sources fully support a mind-bending story about Janus and Epimetheus swapping orbits with 19 cross-verified claims across multiple distinct sources.
story: In 1966, astronomers looking at Saturn spotted a small moon near its rings, naming it Janus. But their tracking data made no sense: the object's calculated position kept shifting unexpectedly. Twelve years later, scientists solved the mystery. Astronomers hadn't been tracking one object, but two distinct moons, Janus and Epimetheus, sharing almost the exact same orbit around Saturn, separated by only 50 kilometers. According to orbital dynamics, two bodies so close should eventually collide. But instead of crashing, Janus and Epimetheus engage in an unprecedented cosmic dance. Every four years, as the inner, faster moon catches up to the outer one, their mutual gravity forces them to trade angular momentum. The inner moon rises outward and slows down, while the outer moon falls inward and speeds up, swapping places without ever colliding. Confirmed by Voyager 1 and Cassini, it remains the only known orbital swap of its kind in the Solar System.
angle: Saturn's moons Janus and Epimetheus share virtually the exact same orbit, trading places every four years in a gravitational do-si-do instead of crashing into each other.

claims.claim: Janus was first identified by French astronomer Audouin Dollfus on December 15, 1966.
Jean Texereau photographed Janus on October 29, 1966, prior to Dollfus's observation, without realizing what he had captured.
Richard Walker observed an object on December 18, 1966, which was later credited as the discovery of Epimetheus.
In October 1978, Stephen M. Larson and John W. Fountain demonstrated that the 1966 observations represented two distinct moons sharing nearly identical orbits.
Voyager 1 confirmed the unique co-orbital configuration of Janus and Epimetheus in 1980.
Janus and Epimetheus swap their inner and outer orbital positions approximately every four years.
The orbital radii of Janus and Epimetheus differ by only about 50 kilometers.
During their closest approach in an orbital swap, Janus and Epimetheus never get closer than roughly 10,000 to 15,000 kilometers from each other.
Janus is approximately four times more massive than Epimetheus, meaning Epimetheus's orbit shifts four times as much during each exchange.
Janus and Epimetheus represent the only known horseshoe orbital swap configuration between moons in the Solar System.
Both Janus and Epimetheus have low densities and high albedos, indicating they are likely icy rubble pile objects.
Scientists suspect Janus and Epimetheus may have formed from the breakup of a single parent moon early in Saturn's history.
Janus acts along with Epimetheus as a shepherd moon, maintaining the outer edge of Saturn's A Ring via a 7:6 orbital resonance.
Meteoroid impacts on Janus and Epimetheus kick up particles that create a faint diffuse dust ring along their orbital paths.
The Cassini spacecraft observed an orbital swap of Janus and Epimetheus in January 2006.
Janus takes approximately 17 hours to complete one orbit around Saturn.
Janus is tidally locked to Saturn, with one side always facing the planet.
The International Astronomical Union officially named the moon Janus in 1983 after the two-faced Roman god of beginnings and doorways.
Major craters on Janus are named after characters in the myth of Castor and Pollux.

disputed: Minimum distance during orbital swap: Wikipedia lists ~10,000 km, whereas NASA Science and Planetary Society list ~15,000 km (9,000 miles). Script should state 'between 10,000 and 15,000 kilometers'.

Origin of the month January: Popular tradition credits the month to Janus, but source S5 states the first month was actually named after Juno. Script should leave out this etymological point to avoid confusion.
